# M06 — Uncertainty quantification (Phase 6)

*Generated by `python -m src.experiments.run_uq` on 2026-07-22 21:18 UTC. Numbers trace to `results/tables/m06_uq_*` and `results/predictions/m06_uq_*.parquet`.*

## Scope

Roadmap Phase 6 (Ch2 §2.6): make the Phase-3 **LSTM** *uncertainty-aware* and test whether its prediction intervals are **calibrated**, on the same leakage-free anchored walk-forward as Phases 2–5 (**RQ3**). Two methods, from the two dominant schools of neural-network UQ, plus one ablation:
- **MC-Dropout LSTM (primary)** — head dropout kept active at inference, **T=100** stochastic passes; the predictive law on log-variance combines the **epistemic** spread across passes with the **aleatoric** residual noise (Gal & Ghahramani 2016), giving a log-normal interval on the variance scale.
- **Quantile-regression LSTM (comparison)** — one LSTM, a monotone (non-crossing) 3-quantile head at τ=[0.05, 0.5, 0.95] trained with the **pinball loss** (Koenker–Bassett 1978; Engle–Manganelli 2004); distribution-free.
- **LSTM-Gaussian (reference)** — the same network's deterministic forecast with an aleatoric-only (no-MC) log-normal interval, i.e. the Phase-3 point model + its residual noise; isolates what the MC passes add.
Hyperparameters are fixed at the Phase-3 selection (hidden 128, lookback 10, lr 1e-3, dropout 0.1); the headline nominal level common to both methods is **90%**.

## Point accuracy is preserved (sanity)

The uncertainty machinery is *added on top of* the Phase-3 point model, so its point forecasts should still land where Phase 3 left them (QLIKE, primary):

| model | n | QLIKE |
|---|---|---|
| LSTM-Gaussian | 784 | 0.2650 |
| LSTM (Phase 3) | 784 | 0.2650 |
| MC-Dropout-LSTM | 784 | 0.2652 |
| Quantile-LSTM | 784 | 0.3216 |


The MC-Dropout predictive mean (QLIKE 0.2652) tracks the deterministic LSTM, and a formal Diebold–Mariano test finds **no** significant point-accuracy difference (DM 1.32, p=0.189) — the intervals come at no cost to the forecast. The **LSTM-Gaussian** point reproduces the Phase-3 LSTM exactly (same weights, dropout off), confirming the reference is the Phase-3 model. The quantile model's higher QLIKE (0.3216) is expected and is *not* an interval-quality signal: its point is the predictive **median**, whereas QLIKE is minimised at the conditional **mean** (Patton 2011), and for right-skewed realized variance the median sits below the mean — so a mean-vs-median QLIKE gap is partly an artefact of the target functional. The quantile method's job is *calibration*, adjudicated below, not point-QLIKE.

## Calibration — central intervals

PICP is empirical coverage (closer to nominal is better); MPIW is mean interval width (smaller = sharper); Winkler is the proper interval score (Gneiting–Raftery 2007, lower better); coverage error = PICP − nominal (negative = over-confident / too narrow).

| method | nominal | n | PICP | MPIW | Winkler | coverage error |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Quantile-LSTM | 90% | 784 | 0.821 | 1.598e-04 | 4.317e-04 | -0.079 |
| LSTM-Gaussian | 90% | 784 | 0.864 | 1.801e-04 | 4.198e-04 | -0.036 |
| MC-Dropout-LSTM | 90% | 784 | 0.865 | 1.818e-04 | 4.199e-04 | -0.035 |
| LSTM-Gaussian | 95% | 784 | 0.920 | 2.287e-04 | 5.660e-04 | -0.030 |
| MC-Dropout-LSTM | 95% | 784 | 0.920 | 2.310e-04 | 5.634e-04 | -0.030 |

## Findings (RQ3)

At the nominal **90%** level, MC-Dropout attains **86.5%** empirical coverage (coverage error -0.035 — over-confident (too narrow)) and the quantile model **82.1%** (-0.079 — over-confident (too narrow)). The MC-Dropout log-normal intervals are the better-calibrated of the two overall, consistent with the literature that MC-Dropout tends to under-cover unless the dropout rate is tuned as a calibration knob (roadmap Risk 4).

**Coverage degrades in the crisis regime — exactly the RQ3 hypothesis.** Both methods cover better in the **calm** state (MC-Dropout 87%, quantile 83%) than in the **crisis** state (MC-Dropout 84%, quantile 80%), where realized variance spikes and the intervals — fit predominantly on calmer history — are caught too narrow. The pooled coverage number therefore flatters both models; the per-regime table is where calibration is honestly adjudicated, and it is the distinctive Phase-6 result.

A structural reading sharpens *why* the two methods differ here. The MC-Dropout predictive band is near-**homoskedastic on the log scale**: its aleatoric term is a single global residual variance estimated once on pre-2019 data and broadcast to every out-of-sample day, and the epistemic term is negligible (below), so the log-normal band is essentially a fixed *multiplicative* factor on the point forecast — it can only widen in crisis to the extent the point forecast itself rises, not because the model has learned that log-RV is intrinsically more dispersed in stress. The quantile head, by contrast, *can* learn a state-dependent width directly from the pinball objective. That the distribution-free quantile intervals still under-cover the crisis more than the parametric ones is therefore the substantive finding — neither device fully solves crisis calibration on 70 COVID-era days, which motivates the Phase-7 combined regime × uncertainty model and a conformal or regime-conditional recalibration as the natural next step.

**Epistemic vs aleatoric.** Averaged over the test window the MC-Dropout predictive std decomposes into an epistemic (model) part 0.045 and an aleatoric (residual-noise) part 0.600 on the log-variance scale — the irreducible noise dominates (0.6% of predictive variance is epistemic). At dropout 0.1 the MC-Dropout and LSTM-Gaussian intervals are therefore close (the reference row confirms it); the substantive calibration contrast is the **distribution-free quantile** method vs the **parametric log-normal** one, and the per-regime breakdown between them. Two modelling assumptions are worth stating plainly: the MC-Dropout interval assumes the log-variance residuals are **Gaussian and homoskedastic** (a single global aleatoric variance), and the epistemic contribution here is small — so this phase should be read as a comparison of *interval calibration* under those assumptions, not as evidence that dropout-Bayesian uncertainty is large for S&P 500 RV.

## Gate criteria

- [x] MC-Dropout LSTM: dropout kept active at inference, T=100 passes, predictive mean + std → log-normal intervals; epistemic/aleatoric variance decomposed.

- [x] Quantile-regression LSTM: monotone non-crossing head at τ=[0.05, 0.5, 0.95], pinball loss; distribution-free intervals.

- [x] Calibration metrics PICP / MPIW / Winkler at 90% (both) and 95% (parametric), with a reliability diagram across a dense τ grid.

- [x] **Per-regime** calibration table (calm / transitional / crisis) for both methods — the RQ3 contribution.

- [x] Point-accuracy preserved vs the Phase-3 LSTM (QLIKE + formal DM); predictions, tables, figures and a reproducible config snapshot persisted.
